title: High School Profit and the District
bigQuestion: When a public school's Friday night game raises and spends money, who should get to see the numbers, and why?

story.title: A Check and an Agenda
story.kicker: On one autumn Friday, a booster club's gift and a school board's budget sit side by side.
paragraphs: Picture a Friday in October at a public high school in Illinois. At five o'clock the ticket booth opens beside the football field. Parents from the booster club sell hot dogs at a stand they built. The marching band warms up behind the bleachers.

At halftime the booster club president walks onto the field. She holds up a large paper check for new scoreboard lights. The crowd cheers. The money came from years of concession sales, raffles and dues paid by parents.

Three days later the school board meets in the library. The meeting is open to the public, as Illinois law requires. Item seven on the printed agenda asks the board to accept the gift. Item eight asks it to approve coaches' extra pay for the season.

Few people who cheered on Friday come to the Monday meeting. Yet the two nights belong together. One is a civic ritual in the stands. The other is the public record of who pays for the lights, the coaches and the field, and how.
story.think: Should the public be able to see how much money a Friday night game brings in and where it goes? Why or why not?

lessons.title: A Thanksgiving Rivalry Since 1882
lessons.mainIdea: Town-against-town high school games, such as Wellesley versus Needham in Massachusetts since 1882, made school sport a public holiday ritual.
reading: Wellesley and Needham are neighboring towns west of Boston. Their high school football teams first played each other in 1882. The game moved to Thanksgiving and is often called the oldest public high school Thanksgiving *rivalry* in the country. Families plan the holiday around it.

In the late 1800s, college football games on Thanksgiving drew large crowds in New York and other cities. High schools copied the custom. A holiday game gave a whole town a reason to gather. Alumni came home, and the game became part of local *identity*.

A ritual like this is *civic*: it belongs to the community, not only to the players. Towns paid for fields and stands, and newspapers printed the scores. The game was public in two senses. It was open to everyone, and it was paid for partly with public money.

words.d: a long, repeated contest between two teams or towns
the sense of who a group of people are and what they share
belonging to a town or community and its public life

look.title: A Game on the Holiday
look.text: It is Thanksgiving morning. Grandparents who graduated fifty years ago sit beside ninth graders. The mayor stands for the anthem. After the game, families drive home for dinner.
look.prompt: What makes this game a civic ritual and not just a sports event?

check.q: When did Wellesley and Needham high schools first play football?
check.why: The two Massachusetts schools first met in 1882.

check.q: What does civic mean?
choices: Belonging to a town or community and its public life
check.why: A civic ritual belongs to the whole community.

check.q: Where did high schools get the custom of Thanksgiving games?
choices: From college football games on Thanksgiving
check.why: The reading says large college Thanksgiving games in the late 1800s gave high schools the custom.

lessons.title: Lights and Public Works
lessons.mainIdea: Electric lights and New Deal building programs in the 1930s helped move high school football to Friday nights at public stadiums.
reading: Early high school games were played on Saturday or holiday afternoons. Electric field lighting became practical and affordable for many towns in the 1920s and 1930s. With lights, a game could start after the workday ended. Working parents could now come to watch.

The Great Depression began in 1929. In 1935 the federal government created the *Works Progress Administration*, or WPA. It hired unemployed workers to build public projects. Among many roads, schools and parks, WPA crews built athletic fields and stadiums for towns and schools across the country.

Many of these stadiums still stand. They were built with federal money, on public land, for public schools. That history matters for the money question today. A Friday night game uses a *public asset*, something owned by the community, even when a booster club pays for new lights.

words.d: a New Deal agency created in 1935 that hired unemployed people to build public projects, including stadiums
something of value owned by the community, such as a school stadium
the severe economic collapse that began in 1929 and lasted through the 1930s

look.title: Who Built the Bleachers?
look.text: A stone plaque on an old high school stadium reads: built by the Works Progress Administration. Beside it hangs a newer sign thanking the booster club for the scoreboard.
look.prompt: What do the two signs tell you about who has paid for this stadium over time?

check.q: What was the Works Progress Administration?
choices: A New Deal agency that hired unemployed people to build public projects
check.why: The WPA, created in 1935, built public works including stadiums.

check.q: Why did lights change who could watch high school games?
choices: Games could start after the workday, so working parents could come
Lights were required by the Supreme Court
check.why: Evening games let working people attend after their jobs.

check.q: What is a public asset?
choices: A private gift to a coach
Something of value owned by the community
A ticket for the best seat
check.why: A public asset, like a school stadium, belongs to the community.

lessons.title: The Prep Bowl at Soldier Field
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Prep Bowl drew huge crowds to Soldier Field, and the 1937 game is often reported as the largest crowd ever for a high school football game.
reading: Soldier Field opened on Chicago's lakefront in the 1920s. It was built by the city's South Park Commission as a memorial to soldiers. For decades it hosted the *Prep Bowl*. This game matched the champion of the Chicago Public League against the champion of the Catholic League.

In November 1937, Austin High School of the Public League played Leo High School of the Catholic League there. The crowd is often reported at more than 100,000 people. Many sources call it the largest crowd for any high school football game in American history. The game was played for charity.

The Prep Bowl joined public and private schools in one city ritual. It also showed that a school game could draw a crowd the size of a college or professional game. Large crowds meant large *gate receipts*, the money from ticket sales. The question of who controls such money has followed school sport ever since.

words.d: Chicago's championship game between the Public League and Catholic League champions, played at Soldier Field
the money collected from selling tickets to an event
giving money to help people in need

look.title: A Crowd the Size of a City
look.text: November 1937: more than 100,000 people, by common reports, fill Soldier Field to watch two Chicago high school teams, one public and one Catholic.
look.prompt: What might a crowd this large have meant for the schools, the city and the charity? Who might have argued over the money?

check.q: Which two leagues' champions met in the Prep Bowl?
choices: The Big Ten and the NFL
The Football League and the Football Association
The Chicago Public League and the Catholic League
check.why: The Prep Bowl matched the Public League and Catholic League champions.

check.q: Which schools played in the famous 1937 Prep Bowl?
check.why: Austin of the Public League played Leo of the Catholic League in November 1937.

check.q: What are gate receipts?
check.why: Gate receipts are ticket-sale money.

lessons.title: Who Invented Homecoming?
lessons.mainIdea: Several colleges, including the University of Illinois in 1910, claim to have invented homecoming, and the record shows the custom spread from colleges to high schools.
reading: Homecoming is a fall weekend when graduates return to see a football game. Several colleges claim to have held the first one. Baylor University in Texas points to 1909. The University of Illinois points to October 1910. The University of Missouri points to 1911.

The Illinois claim rests on a student-organized event built around a game against the University of Chicago. It included a parade and a pep rally. Historians note that each claim uses a different *definition* of homecoming. The honest answer is that the custom grew at several schools at about the same time.

High schools soon copied homecoming, adding parades, dances and a homecoming court. The weekend became a *ritual* that tied graduates to their old school. It also became a time for fundraising. Many alumni gifts and booster drives are still timed to homecoming weekend.

words.d: a fall event when graduates return to their school, usually built around a football game
an exact statement of what a word means; different definitions can lead to different answers
an action repeated in the same way on special occasions because it has meaning to a group

look.title: Three Homecoming Claims
look.cite: Histories published by Baylor University, the University of Illinois and the University of Missouri
look.prompt: All three claims fall within three years. What does that suggest about how the custom began?

check.q: Which year does the University of Illinois claim for its first homecoming?
check.why: Illinois points to October 1910; Baylor claims 1909 and Missouri 1911.

check.q: Why do different schools each claim the first homecoming?
choices: The NCAA gave each a certificate
Each uses a different definition of homecoming
Homecoming was invented by a high school
check.why: Historians note that the claims depend on how homecoming is defined.

check.q: What is a ritual?
choices: An action repeated on special occasions because it has meaning to a group
check.why: A ritual is a meaningful action a group repeats on special occasions.

lessons.title: A Prayer Over the Loudspeaker
lessons.mainIdea: In Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe (2000), the Supreme Court ruled that a public school could not have student-led prayer over the stadium loudspeaker before games.
reading: In the 1990s the Santa Fe Independent School District in Texas had a policy for home football games. Students voted to choose one classmate to deliver a message or *invocation* before each game. The message was spoken over the stadium loudspeaker. Families of some students sued, and they were allowed to use the name Doe to protect their privacy.

The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court. In June 2000 the Court ruled 6 to 3 against the district. The Court said the policy broke the *Establishment Clause* of the First Amendment. That clause bars government from establishing or endorsing religion.

The Court reasoned that the game was a school event on school property. The loudspeaker was school equipment, and the school set up the vote. So the prayer carried the school's approval. The case shows that a Friday night game is a government event under the Constitution, not just a local party.

words.d: a prayer or appeal spoken at the start of an event
the part of the First Amendment that bars government from establishing or endorsing religion
the part of the U.S. Constitution that protects freedom of religion, speech, press and assembly

look.title: The Court's Reasoning
look.text: The Court found that the pregame prayers were delivered on school property, at school-sponsored events, over the school's public address system, under school supervision and by a speaker chosen under a school policy. So they were public speech that the school endorsed.
look.cite: Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe, U.S. Supreme Court, 2000
look.prompt: List the facts the Court used to decide the prayer was the school's speech. Which fact seems strongest to you?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Santa Fe v. Doe in 2000?
choices: The school's pregame prayer policy broke the Establishment Clause
Schools must hold prayers before games
Only coaches may speak on a loudspeaker
check.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 that the policy violated the Establishment Clause.

check.q: What is an invocation?
choices: A prayer or appeal spoken at the start of an event
check.why: An invocation is a prayer or appeal at the opening of an event.

check.q: Why did the Court treat the prayer as the school's speech?
choices: It was printed in a newspaper
It was on school property, over school equipment, under a school policy
check.why: The Court pointed to the school setting, equipment and policy.

lessons.title: A Coach at Midfield, 2022
lessons.mainIdea: In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022), the Supreme Court ruled that a public school coach's personal prayer after games was protected by the First Amendment.
reading: Joseph Kennedy was an assistant football coach at Bremerton High School in Washington State. For years he knelt at midfield after games to pray. Players and others sometimes joined him. In 2015 the school district told him to stop praying where students could join, and it later placed him on leave.

Kennedy sued. In June 2022 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in his favor. The majority said his short, quiet prayer was *private speech* protected by the First Amendment's free speech and *free exercise* clauses. It also set aside an older test courts had used to judge whether government seemed to endorse religion.

The dissent argued that a coach at midfield holds power over players. It said students could feel pressure to join. Read together, the 2000 and 2022 cases show a field where the Constitution applies. The courts drew the line between a school's speech and a person's speech in different places.

words.d: a person's own expression, as opposed to speech the government or school sponsors
the First Amendment's protection of a person's right to practice their religion
a written opinion by judges who disagree with the majority's decision

look.title: Two Cases Side by Side
look.text: Santa Fe, 2000: a student chosen under a school policy prays over the stadium loudspeaker. Bremerton, 2022: a coach kneels alone at midfield after the game and prays quietly.
look.prompt: The Court ruled against the school's policy in one case and for the coach in the other. What differences between the cases did the Court rely on?

check.q: How did the Supreme Court rule in Kennedy v. Bremerton in 2022?
choices: It refused to hear the case
check.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 that the coach's prayer was protected.

check.q: What is a dissent?
choices: An opinion by judges who disagree with the majority
The final score of a game
check.why: A dissent is written by judges who disagree with the decision.

check.q: How is the Bremerton case different from the Santa Fe case?
choices: Bremerton involved a loudspeaker; Santa Fe did not
Both cases were decided the same way
Bremerton was about a coach's personal prayer; Santa Fe was about a school's prayer policy
Santa Fe was about a college; Bremerton about a high school
check.why: Santa Fe struck down a school policy; Bremerton protected a coach's private prayer.

lessons.title: New York's School League, 1903
lessons.mainIdea: In 1903 New York City founded the Public Schools Athletic League, an early model of school sport organized by a city school system with private donors' help.
reading: In 1903 Luther Halsey Gulick Jr. was director of physical training for New York City's public schools. He helped found the *Public Schools Athletic League*, or PSAL. It organized contests among the city's schools. Wealthy donors gave money to get the league started.

The PSAL's founders wanted sport to build health and loyalty among city boys, many from immigrant families. In 1905 a Girls' Branch was added. It favored folk dancing and games over public competition, reflecting ideas of the time about girls and sport.

The PSAL showed a pattern that later spread widely. A public school system ran the league, but private money helped pay for it. That mix of *public* control and *private* funding still shapes high school sport. It is one reason questions about who sees the books can be hard to answer.

words.d: the athletic league of New York City's public schools, founded in 1903
run by or belonging to the government and the community
money that comes from individuals or businesses rather than taxes

look.title: Early School Sport Bodies
rows: New York Public Schools Athletic League
National Federation of State High School Associations
look.cite: Records of the IHSA, the New York City PSAL and the National Federation of State High School Associations
look.prompt: Which came first, the Illinois association or the New York league? What does the chart suggest about when school sport was organized?

check.q: Who helped found New York's Public Schools Athletic League in 1903?
check.why: Gulick, director of physical training for the city's schools, helped found the PSAL.

check.q: What pattern did the PSAL set?
choices: Leagues run only by professional owners
Public control of school sport with help from private money
Sport paid only by federal taxes
check.why: The PSAL was run by the school system but started with donors' money.

check.q: What did the PSAL's Girls' Branch of 1905 favor?
choices: Folk dancing and games over public competition
check.why: The Girls' Branch reflected the era's ideas by favoring dancing and games.

lessons.title: An Association Acts for the State
lessons.mainIdea: In Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA (2001), the Supreme Court ruled that a state high school athletic association made mostly of public schools acts as the state.
reading: The Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association, or TSSAA, governs high school sport in Tennessee. It is a private nonprofit group, but most of its members are public schools. Public school officials sit on its board. In the late 1990s it punished Brentwood Academy, a private school, for breaking a recruiting rule.

Brentwood Academy sued, saying the association had violated its constitutional rights. The key question was whether the TSSAA was a *state actor*. The Constitution limits what government does, not what private clubs do. In 2001 the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that the association was a state actor.

The Court said the association was so tied to public schools and officials that it acted as the state. This matters for *accountability*, the duty to explain and answer for decisions. A body that acts as the state must follow constitutional limits. Many state associations, including the IHSA, are built from public school members in a similar way.

words.d: a person or group whose actions count as the government's under the Constitution
the duty to explain decisions and answer for them to the public
trying to bring players to a team or school

look.title: The Court on the Association
look.text: The Court held that the association's nominally private character was overborne by the pervasive entwinement of public institutions and public officials in its composition and workings.
look.cite: Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association, U.S. Supreme Court, 2001
look.prompt: In your own words, what made the association act like the government, according to the Court?

check.q: What is a state actor?
choices: A person who acts in school plays
A private club with no rules
A person or group whose actions count as the government's
A player on a state championship team
check.why: A state actor's actions count as government action under the Constitution.

check.q: How did the Supreme Court rule in Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA in 2001?
choices: The association was a purely private club
Private schools must leave the association
The association was a state actor, by a 5 to 4 vote
check.why: The Court ruled 5 to 4 that the TSSAA acted as the state.

check.q: Why did the Court see the TSSAA as tied to the government?
choices: Most members were public schools and public officials ran it
It received money from the NFL
It was created by the U.S. Congress
check.why: The Court pointed to its public school members and public officials.

lessons.title: Fees for Playing, 1984
lessons.mainIdea: In Hartzell v. Connell (1984), the California Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not charge students fees to take part in school sports and activities.
reading: In 1978 California voters passed Proposition 13, which sharply limited property taxes. Property taxes paid for much of California's public schools. Budgets tightened. In 1980 the Santa Barbara High School District began charging students fees to join sports teams, bands and other activities.

A parent, Barbara Hartzell, sued. In 1984 the California Supreme Court ruled against the fees. It held that school activities are part of the *free public education* the state constitution promises. Charging fees, the court said, shut out students whose families could not pay.

Many other states have no such ruling, and *pay-to-play* fees are common in some of them. The Hartzell case framed school sport as part of education, not an extra to be sold. That view shapes the argument about profit. If sport is education, its money is public money.

words.d: a 1978 California ballot measure that sharply limited property taxes
schooling that a state promises to provide at no charge to students
fees that students pay to join school sports or activities

look.title: A Fee on the Form
look.text: A 1980 sign-up form for the Santa Barbara school band and sports teams lists a fee for each activity. A family with three children in activities must pay three fees.
look.prompt: Using the reading, explain the court's argument that these fees conflicted with free public education.

check.q: What did Proposition 13 do in 1978?
choices: Sharply limited property taxes in California
check.why: Proposition 13 cut property taxes, which squeezed school budgets.

check.q: What did the California Supreme Court decide in Hartzell v. Connell?
choices: Schools could charge any fee they chose
Only boys' sports could charge fees
Fees for school activities violated the promise of free public education
Sports must be cut from all schools
check.why: The court held activities are part of free public education, so fees were not allowed.

check.q: What is pay-to-play?
choices: A ticket to a Prep Bowl
Fees students pay to join school sports or activities
check.why: Pay-to-play means fees for joining school activities.

lessons.title: A Sixty-Million-Dollar Stadium
lessons.mainIdea: Allen, Texas, opened a public high school stadium costing about $60 million in 2012, and its closing for repairs a year later put school sport spending in the news.
reading: In 2009 voters in the Allen Independent School District, north of Dallas, approved a large *bond*. A bond lets a public body borrow money and repay it over years from taxes. Part of the money built a new high school football stadium. It cost about $60 million and held about 18,000 people.

Eagle Stadium opened in 2012. In 2013 engineers found serious cracks in its concrete, and the district closed it. Games moved elsewhere while the district argued with the builders over who should pay. After repairs, the stadium reopened for games in 2014.

The Allen case drew national attention because it showed how big school sport spending had grown in parts of Texas. Because the bond needed voters' approval, the cost was public from the start. The case shows why *transparency*, openness about money and decisions, matters when public borrowing pays for sport.

words.d: a way for a public body to borrow money and repay it over years, usually from taxes
openness about money and decisions so the public can see them
a local government unit that runs the public schools in an area

look.title: The Ballot Question
look.text: A 2009 ballot in Allen, Texas, asks voters to approve borrowing for new schools and buildings, including a stadium. The debt will be repaid from property taxes over many years.
look.prompt: Why does a vote on a bond make a stadium's cost public in a way a booster gift might not?

check.q: What is a bond?
choices: A way for a public body to borrow money and repay it over years
A contract between a coach and a player
A gift from a booster club
A ticket for the whole season
check.why: A bond is public borrowing repaid over time, usually from taxes.

check.q: What happened to Eagle Stadium in 2013?
choices: It was sold to a professional team
It was closed after engineers found cracks in its concrete
check.why: Engineers found serious cracks, and the district closed the stadium until repairs were done.

check.q: What does transparency mean?
check.why: Transparency means the public can see money and decisions.

lessons.title: Illinois Opens Its Meetings
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois's Open Meetings Act of 1957 and Freedom of Information Act of 1984 let the public watch school boards decide and ask to see their records.
reading: In 1957 Illinois passed the *Open Meetings Act*. It requires public bodies, including school boards, to hold their meetings in public with advance notice. Boards must post an agenda. They may close a meeting only for certain listed reasons, such as some personnel matters.

In 1984 Illinois passed its *Freedom of Information Act*. It lets any person ask a public body for its records. School district budgets, contracts and payments are public records unless a specific exception applies. The law was strengthened in 2010 to make it harder for public bodies to refuse requests.

These laws cover the school district, but a booster club is usually a separate private *nonprofit*. Its own books may not be public records. Money it gives to the school, once the board accepts it, enters district records. The line between the two is often where debates over Friday night money begin.

words.d: a 1957 Illinois law requiring public bodies such as school boards to meet in public with notice
a 1984 Illinois law that lets any person request the records of a public body
an organization that uses its money for its purpose rather than for owners' profit

look.title: Illinois Laws for Public Records
look.cite: Illinois Compiled Statutes, 5 ILCS 120 (Open Meetings Act) and 5 ILCS 140 (Freedom of Information Act)
look.prompt: Which law would you use to see a school board decide, and which to see its spending records?

check.q: What does the Illinois Open Meetings Act require of school boards?
choices: To hold meetings in public with notice and an agenda
check.why: The 1957 law requires public meetings with advance notice and a posted agenda.

check.q: Why might a booster club's books not be public records?
choices: It is usually a separate private nonprofit, not a public body
It is part of the state legislature
Federal law hides all sports money
It is owned by the IHSA
check.why: Booster clubs are usually separate private nonprofits, so FOIA may not reach their books.

check.q: In what year did Illinois pass its Freedom of Information Act?
check.why: Illinois passed its FOIA in 1984 and strengthened it in 2010.

lessons.title: A Disclosure Law for Colleges
lessons.mainIdea: The federal Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act of 1994 requires colleges to publish athletic spending by men's and women's teams, but no such federal law covers high schools.
reading: In 1994 Congress passed the *Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act*, often called EADA. It applies to colleges that take part in federal student aid and have athletic programs. Each year they must report the number of athletes on men's and women's teams. They must also report coaches' pay, revenues and expenses by team.

The U.S. Department of Education makes these reports public. Reporters, researchers and families use them to compare colleges. The law was meant to show whether schools were treating men's and women's sports fairly under Title IX. It uses *disclosure*, making information public, rather than new rules about spending.

No federal law requires the same reports from high schools. Bills to require them have been proposed in Congress but have not passed. Some states and districts publish athletic budgets on their own. So whether the public sees Friday night *revenue* often depends on a local choice.

words.d: a 1994 federal law requiring colleges to report athletic participation and money by men's and women's teams
making information public
money that comes in, such as from tickets, concessions and gifts

look.title: What the Law Requires
look.text: Colleges covered by the act must each year prepare a report listing, for men's and women's teams, the number of participants, operating expenses, coaches' salaries and total revenues, and make it available to students and the public.
look.cite: Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act, 1994, 20 U.S.C. 1092(g)
look.prompt: Which of these reported numbers would help you judge whether a school treats men's and women's sports fairly?

check.q: What does the Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act of 1994 require?
choices: High schools to publish Friday night profits
Colleges to publish athletic numbers by men's and women's teams
Boosters to register with the state
check.why: EADA requires colleges to report participation and money by men's and women's teams.

check.q: What is disclosure?
choices: A rule against playing at night
check.why: Disclosure means making information public.

check.q: Why does whether Friday night revenue is public often depend on local choice?
choices: No federal law requires high schools to report it
The Supreme Court banned such reports
Revenue from games is always zero
Only the NFL can publish it
check.why: EADA covers colleges, and no federal law covers high schools.

review.q: Which case ruled that a state high school athletic association made mostly of public schools acts as the state?
review.why: Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA, 2001, found the association was a state actor.

review.q: How did the WPA shape Friday night football?
choices: It built athletic fields and stadiums with federal money in the 1930s
review.why: The WPA built public projects, including school stadiums, from 1935.

review.q: What do Santa Fe v. Doe and Kennedy v. Bremerton both show?
choices: That high school games are private events
That the Constitution applies to public school games
review.why: Both cases treated games at public schools as settings where the First Amendment applies.

review.q: Why can a booster club's gift be harder for the public to track than a bond?
choices: Boosters are usually private nonprofits, while a bond needs a public vote
review.why: Bonds go to voters; booster clubs usually keep private books until a gift enters district records.

review.q: Which argument did the Hartzell court use against school activity fees?
choices: Activities are part of free public education
Fees were too small to matter
review.why: The court held that activities are part of the free education the state promises.

review.q: What does the Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act cover?
choices: Colleges in federal student aid programs with athletics
review.why: EADA covers colleges that take part in federal student aid and have athletic programs.

review.q: Which pair matches a Chicago event with its year?
choices: Prep Bowl crowd at Soldier Field, 1882
Austin and Leo at Soldier Field, 1937
review.why: Austin played Leo in the Prep Bowl at Soldier Field in November 1937.

review.q: Which Illinois law lets a person ask for a school district's spending records?
choices: The Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act
review.why: The Illinois FOIA of 1984 lets any person request a public body's records.
